cross_tool_domains.attrition: Not applicable / No information: Desk-based secondary legal/policy case study with no primary participant sample or longitudinal follow-up.
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High concern: Pre-existing poverty, HIV/AIDS burden, seasonal drought, water pollution, infrastructure breakdown, and patriarchal household cash control are described narratively without any analytical strategy to separate their effects from those of water policy reform.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Weak: Although the 1998 Integrated Trade and Industry Policy and 2000 National Gender Policy PDFs were inspected directly for gender language, the core water reform instruments (1995 Water Works Act, 1999 Water Resources Management Policy and Strategy, and Article 20 of the Malawian Constitution) are analyzed secondhand via secondary literature and absent from the reference list.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: High concern: Water access, fetching burden, and committee participation rely on unverified secondary statistics (with national safe-water estimates ranging from 47% to 72%), NGO/government web pages, and journalistic anecdotes without standardized primary measurement.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Weak: Gendered water insecurity outcomes (affordability, walking time, water-borne and vector-borne illness, girls' school withdrawal, and governance power) are not empirically measured post-reform and are explicitly framed largely as intended or predicted impacts.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: High concern: No research protocol, systematic search strategy, or formal policy coding scheme is reported; illustrative secondary sources and anecdotes are selectively synthesized to support the paper's theoretical critique.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: High concern: No Methods section, document universe, or literature selection criteria are reported; the Malawi case and supporting academic, donor, NGO, and news sources were selected purposively.

domain_ratings.justification: Core legal and policy instruments examined in the paper—the 1995 Water Works Act, the 1999 Water Resources Policy and Strategy, and Article 20 of the Malawian Constitution—are not cited as primary texts in the reference list and are instead described and quoted secondhand via Mulwafu et al. (2002), Ferguson and Mulwafu (2005), and the 2000 National Gender Policy. Only the 1998 Integrated Trade and Industry Policy and the 2000 National Gender Policy appear to have been consulted directly as online PDFs, without pinpoint statutory section citations.

domain_ratings.justification: Selection of the Malawian case and of supporting academic studies, donor gender audits, NGO web profiles, and journalistic pieces (e.g., Tenthani 2002; Semu-Banda 2007) is purposive and undocumented, creating substantial risk of selective citation aligned with the author's theoretical thesis.

Quantitative figures (such as safe-water access estimates ranging from 72% to 47%, 50% non-functional water points, and up to four daily collection trips) and qualitative quotations are drawn from secondary papers, websites, and news articles without reporting underlying survey designs, definitions, or measurement procedures.

domain_ratings.justification: Replication is severely constrained by the absence of a documented search or analytical method, secondhand reliance on unreferenced water statutes/policies, and dependence on undated or ephemeral NGO, news, and government URLs accessed between 2006 and 2008.

The author advances textual/discourse findings—noting zero mentions of gender or women in the 1998 Integrated Trade and Industry Policy and classifying water-related objectives in the 2000 National Gender Policy around four verbs ('lobby, promote, empower or encourage')—without reporting a formal codebook, document corpus, or systematic coding procedure.

overall_narrative_summary: Marra (2008) is a desk-based single-country legal/policy institutional case study and feminist theoretical synthesis examining how Malawi's post-1995 water policy reforms (principally the 1995 Water Works Act and 1999 Water Resources Policy and Strategy, alongside the 1998 Integrated Trade and Industry Policy and 2000 National Gender Policy) affect rural and impoverished women. Assessed under the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework (structured non-validated judgment, with no numeric score), the study exhibits weak empirical and doctrinal rigor overall (3 'adequate' domains and 10 'weak' domains). Its chief strengths lie in situating the reforms within Malawi's institutional and socio-legal context—highlighting Ministry capacity constraints, male leadership on female-staffed Community Water Boards, household cash-control asymmetries, and matrilineal versus patrilineal regional differences—and directly critiquing vague action verbs in the 2000 National Gender Policy. However, the paper contains no Methods section, no systematic search or document-selection protocol, and no primary empirical data. Crucially, the core 1995 Water Works Act, 1999 Water Resources Policy and Strategy, and Malawian Constitution are analyzed secondhand via secondary literature rather than primary statutory texts, empirical claims rely on secondary reports and journalistic/NGO web sources, and gendered impacts of the water reforms are explicitly framed largely as predicted consequences rather than measured post-reform outcomes.
overall_rating: Weak evidentiary rigor / High risk of bias (structured non-validated judgment under the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework; no numeric composite score)
study_design_identified: Single-country legal/policy institutional case study and secondary narrative policy synthesis (desk-based policy discourse critique and secondary empirical synthesis with no Methods section, no primary fieldwork, and no systematic search)
where_found_summary: Full text reviewed across PDF pp. 1-14 (pp. 161-173; note PDF p. 6 / journal p. 165 contains no body text as prose flows continuously from the bottom of p. 164 to the top of p. 166). Conceptual definitions and feminist theoretical framework appear on PDF pp. 2-5 (pp. 161-164); the Malawi institutional and water context on PDF pp. 5, 7-8 (pp. 164, 166-167); water law reform provisions and prospective gendered impacts on PDF pp. 8-11 (pp. 167-170); constitutional and policy discourse review on PDF pp. 11-12 (pp. 170-171); recommendations and references on PDF pp. 12-14 (pp. 171-173). No standalone Methods section is present.
why_tool_chosen: The study presents a jurisdiction-specific institutional and policy-legal case study ('Case study: Malawi') evaluating Malawian water law reforms and gender policy texts using secondary empirical reports and direct policy-discourse critique of selected government policy documents. It lacks primary qualitative data collection (ruling out CASP), lacks any quantitative analytical sample or quasi-experimental comparator (ruling out ROBINS-I, JBI Cross-Sectional, JBI Cohort, and MMAT), and lacks any systematic search or screening methodology (ruling out AMSTAR 2). The Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework is therefore the matching instrument for appraising its legal source accuracy, institutional contextualization, coding/sampling transparency, and causal support.
